title: Algebraic Analysis of Homomorphic Trace Evaluation and Its Applications
abstract:
Field trace evaluation has emerged as a powerful tool in fully homomorphic encryption, with broad applications ranging from bootstrapping algorithms to privacy-preserving protocols. Recent advances have significantly reduced its noise growth by combining tower-based evaluation strategies with rescaling operations. However, existing analyses rely on uniform noise bounds that fail to capture the actual noise behavior across different coefficients, leading to substantial gaps between theoretical estimates and empirical observations.

In this work, we present a refined algebraic analysis of trace evaluation over power-of-two cyclotomics that uncovers structured cancellation effects among noise coefficients induced by subsequent linear operators, in particular the trace mappings of subextensions. We show that, except for the constant term, the variance of each output noise coefficient depends on the 2-adic valuation of its index, yielding bounds that improve upon prior uniform estimates by a factor of $O(\log n)$ both for non-constant coefficients and after a subsequent plaintext-ciphertext multiplication, where $n$ is the ring degree. We further extend our analysis to two typical algorithmic applications of trace evaluation. For ciphertext packing, we derive a non-recursive formulation that admits a cleaner structure and slightly tighter noise estimates. For coefficient extraction, our coefficient-wise analysis improves upon prior uniform variance bounds by factors ranging from $\Theta(n)$ to $\Theta(n^2)$ for non-constant coefficients and by a factor of $O(n)$ after post-multiplication. Experimental results confirm that the observed noise variances follow the coefficient-wise pattern predicted by our analysis and demonstrate pronounced improvements over existing estimates, providing effective guidance for parameter selection and system configuration in practice.

1     Introduction
Since the groundbreaking work of Gentry [Gen09], fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)
has become a powerful cryptographic tool that allows arbitrary computation on encrypted
data without decryption. To avoid the less standard assumptions underlying Gentry’s
original construction, Brakerski and Vaikuntanathan [BV11a] introduced a more efficient
FHE scheme based on the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem [Reg05], which has been
further extended in subsequent works [BV11b, BGV12] through optimizations including
the use of algebraically structured LWE such as Ring-LWE [SSTX09, LPR10] and General-
LWE [BGV12]. Since then, algebraically structured LWE has become the most popular
foundation for constructing efficient FHE schemes [FV12, DM15, CGGI16, CKKS17].
    In algebraically structured LWE, the underlying basic object is typically taken to be the
ring of integers R of a cyclotomic field K, which has been extensively studied in algebraic
number theory [Lan90, Was97]. One notable improvement from using cyclotomic rings is

the ability to support packed plaintexts, where multiple messages can be encoded into a
single plaintext in R and processed simultaneously. This can be achieved by leveraging
the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) decomposition of R/tR into a direct product of
smaller fields or rings where t is the plaintext modulus [SV14, BGV12, GHS12b, CIV18],
or by utilizing the canonical embedding of K into Cn [CKKS17], where n is the degree
of the field extension K/Q. Both approaches are typical ways to enable SIMD-style
operations on messages encoded in the corresponding slots, thereby significantly enhancing
the throughput of the underlying FHE schemes.

Automorphism Evaluation. Beyond basic homomorphic operations like addition and
multiplication, another crucial operation enabled by the algebraic structure of cyclotomic
rings is the evaluation of automorphisms in the Galois group of K/Q. These automorphisms
can be homomorphically evaluated on ciphertexts [BGV12, GHS12b], allowing for advanced
functionalities such as homomorphic slot-wise rotations in packed plaintexts [BGV12,
SV14, HS14, CKKS17], which are essential for evaluating linear transformations required
in bootstrapping [GHS12a, HS15, CHK+ 18, HS18, BMTH21, MHWW24]. Additionally,
in FHEW/TFHE-type schemes [DM15, CGGI20], automorphisms can be used to multiply
the exponent of a primitive q-th root of unity by units modulo q, an operation underlying
many efficient bootstrapping algorithms [BDF18, LMK+ 23, XZD+ 23, GPvL23, DKMS24,
WWL+ 24, LLW+ 24, XLW24, BJ25, PMH+ 25, GP25, ZWC25]. A distinct recent direction
realizes bootstrapping directly over the automorphism group [HMS25].

Trace Evaluation. The feasibility of automorphism evaluation naturally extends to the
evaluation of the trace mapping from K to its subfield K ′ , which is a K ′ -linear operator
defined as the sum of the Galois conjugates over K ′ . This technique was first used to switch
the underlying algebraic context in BGV-type bootstrapping [GHS12a, GHPS13, AP13]
and was later leveraged to develop efficient algorithms for coefficient extraction [ACLS18]
and ciphertext packing [CDKS21]. These techniques have since been further developed
and used as building blocks in a broad range of cryptographic constructions and appli-
cations [GH19, CCR19, IY21, ALP+ 21, YXS+ 21, MCR21, MW22, RSG+ 22, KLD+ 23,
LHZ+ 23, RCG+ 23, KDE+ 24, BZZ+ 24, ADDG24, MW24, BMW24, HYT+ 24, DFH+ 24,
ACJ24, XW24a, XW24b, LHG+ 25, IB25, BZS+ 25, CR25, LWWC25, CGL+ 25, BI26,
KS26, HZD+ 26, MPSY26, DXQ+ 26, LLT+ 26]. More recently, trace evaluation has emerged
as a useful building block for bootstrapping leveled FHE schemes [OPP23, Gee24, GV26].
It has also found use in a variety of FHEW/TFHE-type bootstrapping algorithms, includ-
ing batch bootstrapping [LW23a, LW23b, LWZ+ 26], functional bootstrapping [XLW24,
XW25, LSL+ 25], and circuit bootstrapping [WWL+ 24, WHS+ 25, LY26].

Efficient Algorithms. In the FHE literature, Alperin-Sheriff and Peikert [AP13] first
suggested exploiting the tower structure of field extensions together with the transitivity to
evaluate the trace mapping more efficiently. An explicit algorithm for the case of power-of-
two cyclotomic fields was later provided in [CDKS21]. For a power-of-two cyclotomic field
K = Q(ζ2n ) where ζ2n is a primitive 2n-th root of unity, the CDKS algorithm evaluates
the trace mapping along the tower K/Q(ζn )/Q(ζn/2 )/ · · · /Q. Since the relative trace of
each degree-two extension in the tower requires only a single non-trivial automorphism
evaluation, the total cost of evaluating the trace TrK/Q is log n automorphism evaluations.
Recall that for any a ∈ K, the trace satisfies TrK/Q (a) = n · a0 where a0 is the constant
coefficient of a. Consequently, after trace evaluation, both the plaintext and the noise are
amplified by a factor of n, a phenomenon commonly referred to as the phase amplification,
which can be undesirable in certain applications. The original work [CDKS21] proposed
to address this issue by multiplying the ciphertext by n−1 ∈ Z∗q prior to trace evaluation,
where q is the ciphertext modulus. However, this approach does not support the case where
n ̸∈ Z∗q , which is precisely the setting adopted by high-performance FFT-based libraries

such as TFHE-rs [Zam22], where q is chosen to be a word-size power of two. To overcome
this limitation, the work [WHS+ 25] proposed applying a modulus switching that rescales
the ciphertext by a factor of 1/n, followed by a modulus raising operation to recover the
original modulus. In this way, the factor n introduced by trace evaluation and the factor 1/n
introduced by modulus switching cancel out, thereby avoiding phase amplification. Very
recently, Lee and Yoon [LY26] further optimized the approach of [WHS+ 25] by splitting the
rescaling factor 1/n into log n successive rescalings by 1/2, with one rescaling performed at
each level of a modified tower. This strategy significantly reduces the additive noise growth
from O(n3 ) to O(n log n). Additionally, efficient trace evaluation for non-power-of-two
cyclotomic extensions has also been studied [ZLW25, XLW24, OPP25, CKL26].

This Work. In this work, we focus on the analysis of trace evaluation over power-of-two
cyclotomics and its applications. Although the work of Lee and Yoon [LY26] significantly
reduces the additive noise growth, their analysis still provides a uniform upper bound
and does not distinguish among different coefficients of the noise term. As a result, these
estimates fail to accurately capture the actual noise behavior across coefficients, especially
for non-constant terms. This loss of tightness becomes particularly evident in applications
that rely on trace evaluation, yet the mechanisms behind it are not fully understood. For
instance, as reported in [MW22], the experimentally observed noise magnitude exhibits a
substantial gap compared to the theoretical estimates. We show that such untightness
arises in part from an algebraic effect not captured by prior uniform analyses:
      Noise terms introduced during homomorphic evaluation are also acted upon by
      subsequent algebraic operators, leading to structured coefficient cancellation.
As a minimal illustrative example, consider the successive homomorphic evaluation of
three linear operators τ1 , τ2 , and τ3 on a ring-based ciphertext c with initial noise e:

Suppose that the evaluation of τ1 , τ2 , and τ3 introduces additive noise terms e1 , e2 , and
e3 , respectively. Prior analyses (e.g., [CDKS21, WHS+ 25, LY26]) use scalar recurrences
to reduce the cumulative action of subsequent operators on each newly introduced noise
term to scalar amplification; our analysis instead retains their exact algebraic action. This
leads to the following contrast for the estimated noise in the final ciphertext c3 :
• Prior Estimate: τ3 ◦ τ2 ◦ τ1 (e) + k1 e1 + k2 e2 + e3 for some amplification factors k1 , k2 .
• Actual Behavior Tracked in Our Analysis: τ3 ◦ τ2 ◦ τ1 (e) + τ3 ◦ τ2 (e1 ) + τ3 (e2 ) + e3 .
In homomorphic trace evaluation, the compositions of the relevant linear operators yield
the trace mappings of subextensions, leading to widespread cancellation of non-constant
coefficients. Motivated by this observation, we develop a coefficient-wise noise analysis
that explicitly tracks the effect of algebraic operators on each coefficient, leading to tighter
coefficient-wise noise estimates for trace evaluation and its applications.

Our Results. By accounting for the effect of algebraic operators on overall noise growth,
we derive tighter noise estimates for trace evaluation and its applications to ciphertext
packing and coefficient extraction. Our main findings are summarized below.
• Trace Evaluation: We show that the noise variances of all non-constant coefficients
  depend on the 2-adic valuations of their indices, yielding an improvement over prior
  uniform estimates [LY26] by a factor of O(log n) both for the non-constant output noise
  coefficients and after a subsequent plaintext-ciphertext multiplication.
• Ciphertext Packing: By reanalyzing the algebraic structure of the algorithm, we pro-
  pose a non-recursive version of the packing procedure in [LY26], which improves

    upon [CDKS21]. This formulation provides a more precise treatment of the overall
    noise, yielding a slightly tighter variance bound than [LY26]. Although this variance
    tightening may be minor in practice, our non-recursive approach offers a cleaner formula-
    tion that may simplify implementation and facilitate further system-level optimization.
• Coefficient Extraction: Similar to trace evaluation, we prove that the noise variances of
  all non-constant coefficients in each output ciphertext depend on the 2-adic valuation of
  their indices and decrease as the valuations increase. Our coefficient-wise variance bounds
  for non-constant coefficients improve upon prior uniform estimates [MW22, BMW24]
  by factors ranging from Θ(n) to Θ(n2 ). Consequently, after plaintext-ciphertext multi-
  plication, our full variance bound improves upon the corresponding bound derived from
  prior uniform estimates by a factor of O(n).
Finally, we provide experimental validation for trace evaluation and coefficient extraction,
where the analytical improvements are pronounced. The observed noise variances are
consistent with our theoretical predictions, supporting both the improvements over prior
work and the specific coefficient-wise noise patterns captured by our analysis.

Applications. We briefly mention two representative applications for which our results
can be directly applied within existing frameworks developed recently:
• Circuit Bootstrapping: The tighter bounds may improve decryption failure estimates,
  enable more favorable parameter choices, or certify a larger remaining post-bootstrapping
  noise margin for subsequent homomorphic evaluations [WWL+ 24, WHS+ 25, LY26].
• Private Information Retrieval: In FHE-based PIR protocols that employ coefficient
  extraction to expand compressed queries [ACLS18, ALP+ 21, MCR21, MW22, BMW24],
  the tighter analysis can support more flexible configurations of the underlying cryp-
  tosystem and may thereby improve key performance metrics.
Beyond these two potential use cases, our results may also be relevant to other applications
built upon trace evaluation, ciphertext packing, or coefficient extraction. More broadly,
our coefficient-wise algebraic analysis shows that tracking how algebraic operators affect
noise throughout homomorphic evaluation can yield tighter bounds. This perspective may
inspire improved design and analysis of other FHE techniques.

Roadmap. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides the
necessary background on cyclotomics and homomorphic encryption. We revisit existing
trace evaluation algorithms in Section 3 and develop our refined algebraic analysis in
Section 4. Section 5 extends this algebraic methodology to the analysis of ciphertext
packing and coefficient extraction, while Section 6 reports our experimental validation.
Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper with remarks on limitations and future directions.

2.2    Basic Encryption Scheme
Now, we review the basics of the encryption scheme used in this work. We begin with the
Ring Learning with Errors (RLWE) problem [SSTX09, LPR10], which is the underlying
problem known to be at least as hard as certain computational problems on ideal lattices.
Definition 1 (Primal-RLWE). For a security parameter λ, let n := n(λ) be the degree of
the ring, let q = q(λ) ≥ 2 be an integer modulus, and let χ = χ(λ) be an error distribution
over R. For s ∈ Rq , the decision version of (primal-)RLWE is to distinguish between
the following two sets of samples: (1) RLWE samples (a, b) ∈ Rq2 where a ← Rq and
b = a · s + e (mod q) for some e ← χ, and (2) uniform samples (a, b) ← Rq2 .

RLWE-Based Encryption Scheme. A typical RLWE-based symmetric-key encryption
scheme consists of the following algorithms:
• ParamGen(1λ ): The parameter generation algorithm takes as input the security pa-
  rameter λ and outputs a parameter tuple params := (n, q, χs , χe ) where n is the ring
  degree, q is the ciphertext modulus, χs is the secret key distribution and χe is the noise
  distribution (typically a discrete Gaussian distribution).
• KeyGen(params): The key generation algorithm takes as input the parameter tuple
  params and outputs a secret key sk := (−s, 1) ∈ Rq2 where s ← χs .
• Enc(sk, m, p): The encryption algorithm takes as input the secret key sk, a message
  m ∈ Rp and a plaintext modulus p, and outputs a ciphertext c := (a, b) ∈ Rq2 where
  a ← Rq and b = a · s + e + ∆ · m (mod q) for some e ← χe and ∆ := ⌊q/p⌉.
• Dec(sk, c, p): The decryption algorithm takes as input the secret key sk, a ciphertext
  c ∈ Rq2 , and a plaintext modulus p, then computes the phase φ = ⟨c, sk⟩ mod q and
  outputs m′ = ⌊(p/q) · φ⌉ mod p.
For convenience, we denote the set of all valid RLWE encryptions of the message m under
the secret key sk and scaling factor ∆ as RLWEsk (∆ · m). When the scaling factor ∆ is
implicit in m or absent, we denote such RLWE encryptions or encodings as RLWEsk (m).
Definition 2 (Noise of RLWE Ciphertexts). For a ciphertext c ∈ RLWEsk (m), the noise
term of c is defined as Err(c) := ⟨c, sk⟩ − m (mod q) with coefficients in [q]± .

5     Algebraic Analyses of Algorithmic Applications
In this section, we explore how our new algebraic insights can be applied to two represen-
tative algorithmic applications of homomorphic trace evaluation: (1) ciphertext packing,
as introduced in [CDKS21] and recently improved in [LY26] with reduced noise growth;

implementations with gcd(n, q) = 1, where the modulus switching/raising steps can be
replaced by exact multiplications by the appropriate inverses modulo q.

6      Experimental Validation
In Sections 4 and 5, we proposed new analyses for trace evaluation and two typical
algorithmic applications by explicitly tracking the effects of algebraic operators. First, we
give a brief summary of the potential implications of our analyses for practical use cases:
• Trace Evaluation: By Theorem 1, the constant-term variance bound matches that
  of [LY26], whereas all other coefficients receive no input-noise contribution and depend
  on the 2-adic valuations of their indices, yielding bounds tighter than the uniform
  estimate by a factor of O(log n). Under the pairwise independence heuristic for the
  output noise coefficients, Corollary 2 further shows that our post-multiplication bound
  is tighter than that derived from the uniform estimate by a factor of O(log n).
• Ciphertext Packing: By Theorem 2, our coefficient-wise analysis gives a slightly smaller
  variance estimate than that of [LY26] due to a more precise analysis of the noise
  introduced by modulus switching. For typical parameter sets where the RLWE secret
  key has a small norm, Vauto dominates Vms , so the variance difference may be small in
  practice. Nevertheless, our non-recursive variant offers a cleaner, more implementation-
  friendly formulation that may facilitate further system-level optimizations.
• Coefficient Extraction: By Theorem 3, the noise variance of the constant term in
  each output is comparable to prior uniform estimates [MW22, BMW24]. However,
  our analysis shows that the variances of all other coefficients depend on the 2-adic
  valuations of their indices, yielding coefficient-wise bounds that are tighter by factors
  ranging from Θ(n) to Θ(n2 ). Under the pairwise independence heuristic for the output
  noise coefficients, the comparison following Corollary 3 shows that the ratio of the
  corresponding uniform estimate bound to ours is O(n).
Therefore, we expect our new analyses to provide more accurate noise estimates, which can
lead to better parameter selection or noise budget management in practical implementations.
To this end, we conduct experiments to validate the asymptotically tighter noise bounds
derived for trace evaluation and coefficient extraction.

7    Concluding Remarks
Extensions. Our improvements arise from an algebraic, coefficient-wise analysis that
preserves structure lost under uniform bounds. This analysis is not tied to the specific
settings considered here and extends directly in the following directions.
• Worst-Case Analysis. The same coefficient-wise algebraic tracking remains applicable
  when worst-case noise bounds are used throughout in place of the average-case variance
  analysis. It can therefore likewise yield tighter bounds than those obtained by uniformly
  bounding all coefficients.
• Intermediate Subfields. This work focuses on full packing/extraction, where the trace is
  taken from K to Q. More generally, the same coefficient-wise insights apply when the
  relative trace targets any intermediate cyclotomic subfield of K.
• NTT Backend. For NTT-based implementations with gcd(n, q) = 1, each modulus-
  switching step followed by modulus raising can be replaced by multiplication by the
  appropriate inverse modulo q. Specifically, the per-level steps use 2−1 ∈ Z∗q , whereas the
  one-shot preprocessing step uses n−1 ∈ Z∗q . These operations are exact and introduce
  no modulus-switching noise; hence, the same analyses apply with Vms = 0.

Limitations. The current estimates rely on the independence heuristic, which is not
exact in general. In addition to dependencies induced by the deterministic structure of
the algorithms, some noise terms share underlying random variables, although they are
treated as independent in our variance estimates. In particular:
• The coefficients of each noise term introduced by an automorphism evaluation are
  heuristically treated as independent in the analysis of coefficient extraction (Theorem 3).
• The coefficients of the output noise from trace evaluation (Algorithm 2) and those
  from coefficient extraction (Algorithm 4) are heuristically treated as independent in the
  subsequent plaintext-multiplication analyses (Corollaries 2 and 3).
In both cases, the coefficients are derived, at least in part, from negacyclic convolutions
involving the same underlying noise coefficients in the automorphism keys, and their
dependence may therefore require a more refined probabilistic treatment. Nevertheless, for
the parameter sets considered in our experiments, the proposed estimates remain above
the empirical variances by a visible margin. For the post-multiplication results, however,
this gap should not be interpreted as a guaranteed safety margin, since the analysis uses
a worst-case bound for the plaintext, whereas the experiments use uniformly sampled
bounded plaintexts and thus reflect typical rather than worst-case behavior.

Potential Refinements. Two main sources of discrepancy between the current estimates
and the actual variances are the independence heuristic and the worst-case bounds for
multiplication in Lemma 3. The latter are used, in particular, to estimate the variance
Vauto of the noise introduced by automorphism evaluation in Lemma 6. The following
directions may therefore further improve the accuracy of the estimates:
• The reliance on the independence heuristic may be reduced by tracking, within the
  present average-case framework, which contributions to the final noise depend on the
  same noise coefficients sampled during automorphism key generation and retaining
  the resulting covariance terms. This refinement could provide more accurate variance
  estimates at the cost of a more involved analysis.
• The worst-case bounds in Lemma 3 may be refined by more accurately characterizing the
  distribution of the gadget decomposition digits, for example by modeling them according
  to an appropriate discrete distribution. Alternatively, one may employ randomized
  gadget decomposition techniques [MP12, AP14, GMP19], for which the coefficients

  after gadget decomposition can be modeled as subgaussian random variables, at the
  cost of requiring additional operations.

probabilistic models and auxiliary bounds adopted here and can therefore accommodate
future advances in noise analysis, potentially yielding more accurate estimates.
